prompt: A colleague proposes testing on the ten best-selling phones in the world this year. What does the section answer?
hint: Whose phones open this app?

choices.text: Agree, since the world's best-sellers are what most of any app's users hold
choices.why: A Brazilian theatre's users keep mid-range phones for years; the world's list is another audience.

choices.text: Start from your own users' phones instead
choices.why: Right. The matrix comes from your analytics, and the market's list tests almost none of them.

choices.text: Test on emulators only, since phones change every year
choices.why: Lesson 19 showed what emulators hide; the question is which devices, not whether.

choices.text: Ten is too few; test the top hundred
choices.why: More of the wrong list is still the wrong list.

prompt: For the Android version dimension, what fixes the oldest value the matrix has to include?
hint: A number in the app's own build.

choices.text: The oldest version the emulator offers
choices.why: The emulator offers many; the app's promise is what matters.

choices.text: The version on the tester's own phone
choices.why: One person's phone is not a promise to users.

choices.text: The app's minimum SDK, 26 for Tickets
choices.why: Right. Below it the app does not install; at it, the app has promised to work.

choices.text: The newest version minus five
choices.why: No rule of that kind exists; the app declares its own floor.

prompt: The matrix has 4 Android versions, 3 screen sizes, 3 makers and 2 languages. A fifth Android version is added. How many combinations does the full product have now?
hint: Multiply the dimensions.

prompt: The coverage script says Android 14, 15 and 13 cover 92.1% of the sessions. What happens to the 3.2% on Android 11?
hint: The section says they do not go away.

choices.text: They are dropped from testing for good
choices.why: They are still users; they are tested less often, not never.

choices.text: They move to the long tail, on rented phones
choices.why: Right. A lighter check, on rented phones, rather than every run.

choices.text: The app's minimum SDK is raised to exclude them
choices.why: That is a product decision about users, not a testing shortcut.

choices.text: They are added to the shelf, since rare versions need a real phone most
choices.why: The shelf holds the oldest supported version where it serves many users, not every rare one.

prompt: In the capture for the model column, how many of the sixteen models are needed to reach 90% of the sessions?
hint: The last line of that capture.

prompt: Why does the section ask you to write the coverage target into the test plan before running the script?
hint: What happens to a target chosen afterwards?

choices.text: Because the script cannot run without a target
choices.why: It defaults to 90%; the reason is about you, not the script.

choices.text: So the analytics tool can filter the export
choices.why: The target is applied after the export, by the script.

choices.text: Because 90% is a legal requirement for apps sold in Brazil
choices.why: No law sets a coverage share; the team chooses it.

choices.text: Otherwise it lands where stopping was convenient
choices.why: Right. Chosen afterwards, the target follows the list instead of judging it.

prompt: In the export, three Android versions reach 90% but it takes eleven models. What should that do to the team's plan?
hint: Which dimension can an emulator vary for free, and which only a phone can?

choices.text: Cover versions on emulators, own a few top models, and rent the model tail
choices.why: Right. Versions are cheap to vary virtually; models are a long tail no shelf holds.

choices.text: Buy all eleven models, since they are what 90% need
choices.why: Lesson 19's argument: phones nobody maintains, and still not the next user's model.

choices.text: Ignore models and test only the three versions
choices.why: Models carry the makers' changes and the hardware the emulator hides.

choices.text: Lower the target to 50% so fewer models are needed
choices.why: That changes the number, not the users who hold the other phones.

prompt: What exactly does a pairwise set promise?
hint: Two at a time.

choices.text: That every combination of all four dimensions is tested
choices.why: That is the full product, 72 rows; pairwise is 12.

choices.text: Any two values of different dimensions meet in some row
choices.why: Right, and nothing about three values at once.

choices.text: That the most used phones are tested first
choices.why: Ordering by use is coverage, section 03; pairwise is about combinations.

choices.text: That a sixth of the defects are found, as 12 is a sixth of 72
choices.why: Coverage of pairs is complete; the fraction of rows says nothing about defects.

prompt: A defect appears only on Android 12, on a Xiaomi tablet, in English. Does the 12-row set of the capture catch it?
hint: Find row 9, and count the values the defect needs.

choices.text: Yes, because every pair of values is covered
choices.why: The defect needs three values together, and pairs do not promise that.

choices.text: Yes, in row 9
choices.why: Row 9 is Android 12, tablet, Xiaomi, in Portuguese.

choices.text: No: no row holds all four values
choices.why: Right. The defect needs four values at once; row 9 has three of them, in Portuguese. This is what the section said pairwise gives up.

choices.text: No, because tablets are left out of pairwise sets
choices.why: Three rows of the set are tablets.

prompt: No pairwise set for this matrix can be shorter than 12 rows, because the four Android versions and the three screens alone make ___ pairs, and each row holds one of them.
hint: Four times three.

prompt: Match each thing a pairwise tool such as PICT adds to what it means.
hint: The list at the end of the section.

pairs.right: combinations that do not exist are left out
every three values together, for the dimensions you fear most
rows you must have are kept and built around

right_distractors: rows are sorted by how many sessions they have

prompt: Which of these can you count on from a device cloud, according to the section?
hint: What comes back, and what is somebody else's policy?

choices.text: A video of the screen for each run
choices.why: Right, and it is what settles a failure.

choices.text: The device's log and screenshots
choices.why: Right: more than a phone on your desk records by itself.

choices.text: A guarantee that the last customer's data is gone
choices.why: Cleaning is the vendor's policy to read, not a guarantee to assume.

choices.text: Your computer's localhost, reachable from the phone
choices.why: Neither localhost nor 10.0.2.2 means your computer there; a tunnel or a public test server is needed.

prompt: Tickets, uploaded unchanged to a cloud's real Galaxy A15, shows "Could not reach the box office". boxoffice runs on your laptop. Why?
hint: What does baseUrl say, and what does it mean from that building?

choices.text: The cloud blocks plain HTTP for security
choices.why: Android's own rule allows 10.0.2.2 in Tickets; the address is the problem, not the protocol.

choices.text: baseUrl is 10.0.2.2, which means nothing on that phone
choices.why: Right. The build needs a reachable test server, or the cloud's tunnel back to your laptop.

choices.text: The Galaxy A15 runs a version of Android too new for Tickets
choices.why: Tickets runs from API 26 upwards; the request failed, not the install.

choices.text: boxoffice refuses requests from phones
choices.why: boxoffice answers anything that reaches it; this request never did.

prompt: A test run on a cloud phone needs to sign in. Which of these follows the section?
hint: Whose phone is it, and who sees the video?

choices.text: Your own account, since it is only for a few minutes
choices.why: A rented phone, a stored video: your own data has no place there either.

choices.text: A customer's account, so the test sees real data
choices.why: Real customers' data on a rented phone is exactly what the LGPD warns about.

choices.text: A test account, with its password as an environment variable of the run
choices.why: Right: test data only, and the secret never in the code or typed on screen.

choices.text: A test account, its password written in the test file
choices.why: Written in the file, it leaks with the code; lesson 3 said why a secret never goes there.

prompt: A 10-minute suite runs every night on section 04's 12 rows, with 2 devices allowed in parallel. How long does the night's run take, and how many device minutes does it bill?
hint: Parallelism shortens the night; it does not shorten the bill.

choices.text: 120 minutes, and 60 device minutes
choices.why: The two numbers are swapped: parallel devices halve the time, not the minutes.

choices.text: 10 minutes, and 120 device minutes
choices.why: That needs 12 devices at once, not 2.

choices.text: 60 minutes, and 60 device minutes
choices.why: Each of the 12 rows still bills its own 10 minutes.

choices.text: 60 minutes, and 120 device minutes
choices.why: Right: twelve runs of 10 minutes, two at a time.

prompt: Lesson 15's Appium test is moved to a cloud. What changes in it?
hint: Where it connects, and what it installs.

choices.text: Every locator, since cloud phones expose different ids
choices.why: The app's ids are the same on any phone; the tests stay as written.

choices.text: The remote() call and the app's id
choices.why: Right: the server, the account, the uploaded app, the row's device and version, and the seats request now asking the server the phone reaches.

choices.text: The language, since clouds only run Java tests
choices.why: Appium speaks HTTP; any client language works.

choices.text: Nothing: a cloud runs a test file as it is
choices.why: It has to connect to the cloud's server and name the uploaded app.

prompt: In the Firebase Test Lab command, what does each --device line stand for?
hint: Model, version, locale, orientation.

choices.text: A phone connected by USB to your computer
choices.why: Test Lab's phones are in Google's data centre.

choices.text: A test class to run
choices.why: The test APK holds the tests; --device chooses where they run.

choices.text: One row of the matrix
choices.why: Right, so twelve rows are twelve --device lines.

choices.text: A retry of the previous device
choices.why: Retries have a flag of their own; --device names a configuration.

prompt: A cloud run fails on one row. Put the section's steps in order.
hint: The cheapest look first.
items: watch the video at the failing step
compare the row with its neighbours
file the defect with the build it came from

prompt: What goes in `appium:app` when the session runs on a cloud's server?
hint: Where is the APK by then?

choices.text: The id the upload returned
choices.why: Right. The cloud answered the APK's upload with an id; the APK is already on its side, and the session names it.

choices.text: The APK's path on your disk, as in lesson 15
choices.why: The cloud's server cannot read your disk.

choices.text: The app's package name, example.tickets
choices.why: The package name says which app, not which uploaded file to install.

choices.text: Your access key
choices.why: The key goes in key, from the environment; never in a capability.

prompt: After reading the export, a manager wants to buy the eleven models that cover 90%. What do you propose instead?
hint: Lessons 19 and 20 together.

choices.text: Buy them, and add the five rare ones later
choices.why: Sixteen phones nobody maintains, and next year's models still missing.

choices.text: Buy none and rely on emulators for everything
choices.why: Emulators hide the device-only rows of lesson 19's table.

choices.text: A shelf of two or three chosen phones, the model tail rented in a cloud, versions on emulators
choices.why: Right: each place doing the rows it is good at, and the export picking the rented models from the top.

choices.text: Buy the single most used model, the Galaxy A15
choices.why: One phone of one maker mistakes that maker's habits for Android's.

prompt: A nightly cloud run fails on one row, a Moto G24. The video shows the list never loading. Run again, the row passes; the other rows passed both times. What do you do?
hint: Step 2 of the section's reading order.

choices.text: File a defect on Motorola phones
choices.why: It did not repeat, and a defect on a model repeats.

choices.text: Remove the Moto G24 from the matrix
choices.why: It is the third model by use; dropping it drops its users.

choices.text: Add a sleep before every step of the suite
choices.why: A fixed sleep slows every row and fixes nothing; lesson 15 waits for elements instead.

choices.text: Treat it as the network or the cloud, note it, and watch whether it comes back
choices.why: Right. A failure that does not repeat is not the app on that phone; a pattern over nights would be.

prompt: The matrix grows a fourth maker. A teammate says the pairwise set will need 96 rows now, a third more than 72. What is wrong with that?
hint: 96 is a product. What does pairwise count?

choices.text: Nothing: pairwise grows with the full product
choices.why: The full product grows to 96; a pairwise set grows with the pairs.

choices.text: 96 is the full product, not the pairs
choices.why: Right. Pairwise grows with the pairs, far more slowly: Android's four versions with four makers set a floor of 16, nowhere near 96.

choices.text: It should be 72 still, since pairwise never grows
choices.why: More values mean more pairs, so the set does grow, slowly.

choices.text: A fourth maker cannot be added to a pairwise set
choices.why: Any number of values can; the script would take the new list as it is.
